explanations.explanation: That's his point, friend. Paul says, “Everything is permissible…” but not everything is beneficial. So "allowed" and "helpful" are two different questions, and he wants them both asked. I'm allowed to eat a whole tray of warm cookies, but my apron strings would file a complaint.

Close, but that one runs backward. Paul starts with “Everything is permissible…” and then says not everything is beneficial. The question he raises is about things that are allowed but still not helpful. He never says helpful things get banned.

Paul doesn't throw the saying out. He lets “Everything is permissible…” stand and then adds that not everything is beneficial, and not everything is edifying. He's adding a second question, not shutting every door. If nothing were allowed, my bakery would be awfully quiet.

Yes! Paul says, “No one should seek his own good, but the good of others.” (1 Corinthians 10:24) He points everyone's eyes away from their own plate and toward the person next to them. In my bakery, that means the first cookie goes in somebody else's box, not my apron pocket.

Paul says the opposite here. His words are, “No one should seek his own good, but the good of others.” (1 Corinthians 10:24) I've tried the sneak-the-first-cookie-off-the-tray plan myself, friend. The tray always notices.

Paul doesn't mention teachers at all. He says, “No one should seek his own good, but the good of others.” (1 Corinthians 10:24) "Others" is a wide-open word, and it's not a short list of important names. Think of whoever happens to be standing across the table from you.

That's it. Paul says, “Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience…” (1 Corinthians 10:25) So no worrying over every package. He gives his reason in the very next verse.

explanations.answer: Ask where it came from first
explanations.explanation: Paul says to skip the questions. His words are “…without raising questions of conscience…” (1 Corinthians 10:25) No cross-examining the seller like a detective with a clipboard, friend. Just buy it and eat.

explanations.answer: Skip all of it to be safe
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't tell anyone to skip the market. He says, “Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience…” (1 Corinthians 10:25) "Anything" is a big word, and he means it. Walking out with an empty cart isn't what he's after.

Yes, the Lord. Paul quotes it: “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.” (1 Corinthians 10:26) It comes from Psalm 24:1. Everything in that market sits inside what belongs to Him. That's the reason Paul gives.

Angels don't show up in this verse, friend. Paul quotes, “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.” (1 Corinthians 10:26) That's from Psalm 24:1. The owner named there is the Lord Himself, and nobody else is on that deed.

No kings in this one, friend. Paul quotes, “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.” (1 Corinthians 10:26) He's pulling from Psalm 24:1. The owner named there is the Lord, and no king gets a crumb of the credit.

True! Paul says, “If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat anything set before you without raising questions of conscience.” (1 Corinthians 10:27) Notice that the believer in this scene wants to go. Once you're there, you can eat without quizzing the host.

This one's actually true. Paul says, “If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat anything set before you without raising questions of conscience.” (1 Corinthians 10:27) So at that table, the believer can eat what's served. No interrogating the host before you sit down.

Right. Once someone tells you the food was offered to idols, Paul says, “then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience…” (1 Corinthians 10:28) The moment someone says that out loud, the answer changes. The two reasons he gives are the person who spoke up and conscience.

That fits the verse before this one, where Paul says to eat what's set before you. In this verse, though, someone tells you the food was offered to idols, and Paul says, “then do not eat it…” (1 Corinthians 10:28) What's different is that someone tells you. Same meal, different instructions.
Paul doesn't leave room for a polite nibble. He says, “then do not eat it…” (1 Corinthians 10:28) A little bite is still eating, friend, and the crumbs would give you away.

Careful, this one flips. Paul says it's “…the other one’s conscience, I mean, not your own.” (1 Corinthians 10:29) So the conscience in view is the person who spoke up. Yours isn't the one he's talking about.

Yes, False. Paul says to skip it for the sake of “…the other one’s conscience, I mean, not your own.” (1 Corinthians 10:29) Right there in the verse he says whose it is: the other one's, not yours. The conscience at stake belongs to the person who said something.

That's the one. Paul says, “So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31) Eating, drinking and everything else all land under that one line. Nothing in your day falls outside it.

The church does show up, but in the next verse and for a different reason. There Paul says not to become a stumbling block to “…the church of God…” (1 Corinthians 10:32) The glory in verse 31 goes to God: “…do it all to the glory of God.” Easy to mix up, since they sit side by side.
Paul doesn't point the glory at the apostles. He says, “…do it all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31) The credit goes straight to God. Nobody else gets the spotlight.

That's not what he says. Paul writes, “Do not become a stumbling block, whether to Jews or Greeks or the church of God…” (1 Corinthians 10:32) That's three groups, and the church is only the last one named. The warning covers people outside the church too.

Yes, False. Paul says, “Do not become a stumbling block, whether to Jews or Greeks or the church of God…” (1 Corinthians 10:32) He names three groups, and the church is just one of them. Jews and Greeks are in there too, so it isn't only about fellow believers.
Saved, yes. Paul says, “…I am not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved.” (1 Corinthians 10:33) That's the goal he states. He's after the good of many, not his own.
Nope, impressed isn't the word. Paul says he's “…not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved.” (1 Corinthians 10:33) Impressing people isn't on his list. Being saved is.

Rewarded sounds nice, friend, but it's not the word here. Paul says, “…I am not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved.” (1 Corinthians 10:33) The goal he names is that people be saved. Not a prize, not a pat on the back.

Christ it is. Paul says, “You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1) So he points past himself to the One he's following. I'm glad that's how it goes, because my mustache is not a safe thing to imitate.

Moses, who brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), doesn't come up in this verse. Paul says, “You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1) The one Paul follows is Christ. He points to Him, not to any of the famous names from the old days.

Abraham is a big name, and I get why it jumped out at you. Big names grab the eye, friend, like the biggest cookie on the cooling rack. But look at what Paul says right before this: he isn't seeking his own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved. (1 Corinthians 10:33) Then he says, “You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1) Christ is the One he follows, and Abraham isn't named anywhere in this passage.
